title: Schools White Paper: making big plans work in real places
label: 15 September 2026 · Schools White Paper evidence
summary: MPs questioned local government and school leaders about the Schools White Paper. Witnesses said the plan has many good aims—better special needs support, more technical routes, more enrichment and a stronger focus on belonging—but warned there are too many new commitments at once, not enough money, and practical problems in rural areas, with falling pupil numbers, unclear accountability for academy trusts, and persistent issues with attendance and behaviour. The witnesses urged careful sequencing, local flexibility, better funding, and stronger local partnerships to deliver the reforms.

chapters.title: Too many changes at once—sequencing and funding matter
chapters.takeaway: The White Paper has lots of good ideas but contains too many separate commitments to implement all at once; sequencing and extra funding are crucial.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The White Paper has many reforms. How should government make sure schools aren't overwhelmed? What should be prioritised?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: The School's White Paper lists about 100 separate commitments. That creates a real risk of overburdening schools unless reforms are sequenced, clearly planned and funded.

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: The Local Government Association agrees. Local councils can help deliver parts of the plan—like enrichment—so flexibility and a sensible timetable are important.

turns.speaker: Jess Asato
turns.text: Is there a big risk if we try to do everything at once?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Yes. But there is also risk in doing nothing—especially with the special educational needs reforms, which are vital for this generation.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So ministers should identify a smaller number of priorities, give money, and make a realistic timetable?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Exactly. And they should use local councils' capacity where it exists, rather than insisting on a one-size-fits-all approach.

chapters.title: Technical routes, work experience and devolution: place matters
chapters.takeaway: Improving technical qualifications and two-week work experience is sensible, but rural areas, weak local job markets and unclear devolution arrangements make delivery hard without local coordination and funding.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: The new Government wants stronger technical pathways in schools. Are those deliverable, especially for places with few local employers?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: They're welcome, but they won't work by themselves. Young people need real job opportunities afterwards—local economies and employer demand matter.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: The technical awards at 16 currently lack consistent national standards and rigour. The Department could speed up work to strengthen these awards and align them with post-16 technical options.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: What about rural areas with few colleges and employers?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Rural places will need more relationship-building and support—transport and access are big issues. Government should not lock young people into narrow choices at 14.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The White Paper also suggests devolution for skills—how will that affect local government?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Devolution can help solve 'place' problems, but questions remain about places without a mayor and how funding and powers will be shared between councils and new regional bodies.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Multi-academy trusts can act as local civic leaders too; strong place-based partnership across councils, trusts and employers is what’s needed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: On work experience, the LGA says two weeks for every child is ambitious—do you stand by that?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: It's a worthy aim, but delivery needs funding and employer engagement, especially in rural areas.

chapters.title: Trusts, governance and parental trust: the accountability gap
chapters.takeaway: Some academy trusts have improved struggling schools, but parents often feel disconnected; trusts face heavy financial rules, yet local accountability and clearer routes for schools to change trust membership need fixing.

turns.speaker: Jess Asato
turns.text: The Government wants all schools in strong trusts. Is there clear evidence trusts improve schools?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Our research shows sustained improvement over time, especially in disadvantaged areas, though results vary between trusts. We can’t yet claim full causation, but the trends are positive.

turns.speaker: Jess Asato
turns.text: Parents tell MPs they feel there's nowhere to take complaints once an individual headteacher has dealt with them. Trusts can seem distant—how do we fix that?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Trusts have strong financial reporting obligations (they publish accounts and are audited). But local governance matters: trusts should build local boards or contacts so parents feel connected.

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: I get the same emails from parents. Some trusts and maintained schools both have work to do on transparency, but inspections that look across a whole trust could help.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What about councils forming their own trusts?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Councils shouldn't be forced to form trusts. Many maintained schools are already rated good or outstanding; forming trusts can risk local conflicts and financial strain for councils with many small schools.

turns.speaker: Peter Swallow
turns.text: When schools join a trust and later want to move to a different local trust, current rules can trap them. Should government join the place agenda with practical rules on trust membership?

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: Yes—governance must give local volunteers real agency. Some trusts grew through competition and empire-building; we need ways to re-align schools to the right local partnerships.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So ministers should give clearer rules and tools to let schools move into genuinely local arrangements?

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: Exactly. The goal should be collective accountability so children don't fall through the cracks, whether services sit in a trust or the council.

chapters.title: Enrichment, the school day, attendance and behaviour—relationships first
chapters.takeaway: Enrichment and belonging help learning, but schools need funding, sensible expectations about the school day, and better support for behaviour and attendance rooted in relationships, not punishment.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: The Government wants more enrichment (things like art, music, sport) and has money for programmes such as Every Child Can and HAF—the Holiday Activities and Food programme. What more is needed?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: HAF works well, and councils' libraries and leisure services can help. But schools need funding and transport support—especially rural and special schools—to make enrichment genuinely inclusive.

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Enrichment builds joy and belonging. The system mustn’t cut it because schools are overloaded by reform; more money would help make enrichment universal.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: Should we talk about a longer school day to fit more in?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Context matters: some schools have extended days to meet community needs, but it shouldn’t be mandated from the centre. It raises workforce and transport questions.

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: Belonging means everyone feels known and supported. That reduces exclusions and improves attendance. It’s not a soft extra, it’s part of the core job of schools.

turns.speaker: Mrs Brackenridge
turns.text: Persistently absent pupils are a serious problem. Should we support first and punish later?

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: Yes—penalties hit the poorest families hardest. We need to understand why a child is missing school and offer support: trauma-aware approaches and relationships-focused work help.

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: We also need to rebuild the relationship between schools and parents. During Covid many relationships shifted. Schools that model good behaviour and give pupils agency are getting better outcomes.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: Teachers say bad behaviour is pushing them out of the profession. Should initial teacher training teach more about trauma and attachment?

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: Absolutely—teachers need more training to spot and respond to trauma and to use relational approaches, so classrooms are calmer and safer for everyone.

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: Beware of blunt tools: tying attendance targets to inspections can have perverse effects. Pupils with additional needs can be unfairly penalised if context isn’t understood.

chapters.title: Accountability, funding and priorities—pick the game changers
chapters.takeaway: Ministers should narrow down priorities, fund them properly, balance national standards with local flexibility, and make accountability and funding decisions that encourage schools to work together for disadvantaged children.

turns.speaker: Peter Swallow
turns.text: On accountability, the Government has suggested changing Progress 8 (the measure of pupil progress across a set of GCSEs). Is that the right way to widen the curriculum?

turns.speaker: Leora Cruddas
turns.text: Progress 8 (a measure that compares pupil progress across English, maths and other subjects) matters. No measure is perfect—adding breadth is sensible, but it's a technical trade-off and we should see the details first.

turns.speaker: Peter Swallow
turns.text: And funding: should disadvantage funding be targeted centrally or should local areas have flexibility?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Councils want flexibility because they know local needs, but we’ll confirm the LGA position in writing—schools need predictable, fair funding that follows need.

turns.speaker: Darren Paffey
turns.text: Falling pupil rolls are real. Do local authorities need more powers to plan places when some schools academy-ise and sidestep local plans?

turns.speaker: Councillor Oliver
turns.text: Local authorities need backstop powers to ensure enough places and fair placements, regardless of whether schools are maintained or in trusts.

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: There’s too much in the White Paper—104 new asks. Ministers should choose a few game changers: better key stage 3 (early secondary years), sorting the GCSE 'forgotten third' who get low passes, and giving vocational routes genuine status.

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: PISA international test results are imperfect and get politicised. We shouldn't over-react; focus on fixing what hurts pupils locally—attendance, belonging and meaningful qualifications.

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: If government wants schools to be community anchors, it must clarify what that means, empower local governance and listen to volunteers and parents in each place.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If you could give ministers three things to listen to, what would they be?

turns.speaker: Sam Henson
turns.text: Define 'community anchor' clearly and involve local governors, volunteers and parents in making it real.

turns.speaker: Dr Thompson
turns.text: Support schools as they change culture—relational work takes time and they mustn't be punished during that transition.

turns.speaker: Geoff Barton
turns.text: Re-empower headteachers: give them room to focus on the few things that will make the biggest difference for disadvantaged pupils and judge them on that.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. Please send any written follow-up evidence—this Committee will press for clear plans, money and sensible sequencing.
